nature-eco-305.title: Trophic levels: counting the steps from sunlight
nature-eco-305.text: Of all the sunlight that reaches plants, only about 0.001% ends up in a tertiary consumer, a meat-eater that eats other meat-eaters. Plants turn about 1% of the sunlight they receive into chemical energy. Consumers then convert, on average, only about 10% of the energy in their food into their own tissue. That is why feeding chains rarely exceed 5 or 6 levels. Each step is a trophic level. It is an organism's position in the network of who eats whom, counted in feeding steps from the start of the chain. Level 1 is primary producers such as plants. Level 2 holds the plant-eaters, the primary consumers. Carnivores that eat them are secondary consumers, and carnivores that eat carnivores are tertiary consumers. Top predators typically sit at level 4 or 5. Organisms get food in three basic ways: as producers, as consumers, or as the organisms covered in {{ref:nature-eco-340}}. Raymond Lindeman developed the concept in 1942, building on August Thienemann's 1926 terms producers, consumers and reducers. The idea reaches into markets. Fish at higher trophic levels usually fetch more money, which can lead to heavy fishing at those levels. Humans have a mean trophic level of about 2.21, about the same as a pig or an anchovy.

nature-eco-359.title: Herbivores: the animals that eat plants
nature-eco-359.text: Over-browsing, eating too many shoots and leaves, by white-tailed deer in the US could cost projects that restore forests more than $750 million a year. Deer are herbivores: animals adapted to eat plants, such as leaves, fruits or seeds, as the main part of their diet. Herbivores are primary consumers. They eat the carbohydrates plants make from sunlight, and carnivores in turn eat them. Plant food is hard to digest. Many herbivores rely on gut bacteria and protozoans to break down cellulose, which is much harder to digest than animal tissue. Herbivores shape plant diversity. Abundant deer reduce the number of plant species, while bison hold back dominant plants so others can flourish. When predators decline, unchecked herbivores can over-forage and suppress plant communities. Some plant-eating even helps plants: carrying seeds and pollen feeds the animal while helping the plant reproduce.

nature-eco-353.title: Food chains: who eats whom, in a single line
nature-eco-353.text: A green plant is eaten by a snail, the snail by a frog, the frog by a snake, and the snake by an eagle. That is a food chain: a single linear path through a {{ref:nature-eco-297}}. It usually starts with a producer such as grass or algae and ends with a top predator or an organism that breaks down the dead. It shows who eats whom, level by level. When many food chains interconnect, they form that larger, tangled network. A chain's base is primary producers, which make organic compounds from sunlight or from inorganic chemicals. Every other member is a consumer. In dark places such as hydrothermal vents, bacteria and archaea that use hydrogen sulfide and methane form the base. When organisms die, detritivores and other breakers-down of remains turn them into simple nutrients that return to the soil for plants. Food chains also trace pollution. In ecotoxicology, the study of poisons in ecosystems, they show how contaminants pass along and biomagnify, building up at each step. Removing even one link can push other species toward extinction.

nature-eco-297.title: Food webs: the tangled network of who eats whom
nature-eco-297.text: Losing one species can harm a whole chain of others, a knock-on loss described in {{ref:nature-eco-106}}. The reason is the food web, the network of linked food chains in a community that shows who eats whom. Organisms are broadly classed as autotrophs, which make their own food, or heterotrophs, which feed on others. Feeding links fall roughly into four kinds: herbivory (plant-eating), carnivory, scavenging and parasitism. Plants form the base. Top predators sit at the summit, where nothing kills them for food. Energy and matter move differently through a web. Energy moves one way, and eventually all of it is lost as heat. Materials such as nutrients cycle round and round. A food chain usually has at most four or five links, and chains in water are often longer than those on land. Charles Elton's 1927 book Animal Ecology made food chains and food cycles central to ecology.

nature-eco-301.title: Keystone species: small numbers, outsized effects
nature-eco-301.text: When the zoologist Robert T. Paine removed ochre starfish from rock pools, mussels took over. The number of clinging species fell from 15 to 8 within three years, and ten years later mussels largely filled the pools. Paine introduced the idea of the keystone species in 1969. It names a species whose effect on its surroundings is far larger than its numbers would suggest. Like the keystone of an arch, it may be a small part of the ecosystem by biomass, yet removing it can trigger a dramatic shift. Sea otters are a famous case. When fur hunting cut them to fewer than 1000 in the north Pacific, sea urchins grazed away the kelp, the underwater forests described in {{ref:nature-eco-422}}. Reintroducing otters restored them. In Greater Yellowstone, removing gray wolves led to overgrazing that hurt beavers and streams. After wolves returned, the riverside ecosystem recovered within a few years. Some keystones help rather than hunt: certain seeds will not grow unless they have passed through a cassowary. The concept overlaps with indicator and umbrella species and with {{ref:nature-eco-116}}, and it has helped ecologists talk to conservation policymakers. One researcher listed 230 species called keystones in about 157 studies over the 50 years since Paine's paper. Critics say the term oversimplifies complex ecosystems, has been stretched to many meanings and depends on local context.

nature-eco-380.title: Predation: the hunter and the hunted
nature-eco-380.text: Lynx and snowshoe hare numbers rise and fall in cycles, and the way predators and prey interact may explain why. Predation is an interaction in which one organism, the predator, kills and eats another, its prey. It belongs to a family of feeding behaviors along with parasitism and parasitoidism. It overlaps with herbivory when animals destroy seeds. To feed, a predator must search for, pursue and kill its prey, weighing costs and benefits at each step. Predators limit prey both by eating them and by changing how they behave. Without predators, a prey population can grow exponentially until it nears its {{ref:nature-eco-593}}. Predators also shape ecosystems indirectly by changing herbivore behavior, as wolves do for riverside plants and sea otters for kelp. By stopping any one species from becoming dominant, some predators raise biodiversity. Such predators are called keystone species.

nature-eco-321.title: Apex predators: the hunters at the top
nature-eco-321.text: After gray wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone in 1995, elk declined and changed their behavior. Willows, aspens and cottonwoods flourished, creating habitat for beavers and moose. Wolves are apex predators: predators at the top of a food chain with few or no natural predators of their own. They occupy the highest trophic levels. Chains on land are shorter, so wolves mostly eat large herbivores that eat plants. Apex predators are central to how ecosystems function, to regulating disease and to maintaining biodiversity. Those that control the levels beneath them are often considered keystone species. Humans have hunted many apex predators close to extinction. {{ref:nature-hist-007}} now threatens others, such as the polar bear, by shrinking Arctic sea ice. Tourism sometimes relies on apex predators, and efforts to restore wild species have reintroduced the Iberian lynx. Bringing back large predators is controversial, partly because farmers fear for their livestock.

nature-eco-407.title: Trophic cascades: when removing one level reshapes all
nature-eco-407.text: Remove the fish-eating fish from a lake, and the water can turn from clear to green as phytoplankton flourish. That is a trophic cascade: a chain of indirect effects through a food web that follows when one feeding level is suppressed. It can reshape a whole ecosystem. In a top-down cascade, predators cut prey numbers or change prey behavior, which frees the level below. Remove the top predators, and consumers can overrun the producers. {{ref:nature-hist-051}} first described the mechanism after seeing deer overgraze mountains once wolves were exterminated. Examples now span the seas. Where sea otters were hunted out, sea urchins increased and kelp declined. In the Baltic Sea, heavy fishing of Atlantic cod let its prey, sprat, take over. The sprat then reduced the copepods, tiny crustaceans, that they eat. Yellowstone's wolf reintroduction is popularly cited as a cascade. Yet that ecosystem is too complex and open to be a straightforward example. Ecologists agree that cascades exist. How widespread they are has long been debated.

nature-eco-409.title: Energy flow: one-way traffic through living things
nature-eco-409.text: Energy enters living things once and never comes back around, as {{ref:nature-eco-297}} showed. Energy flow is the movement of that energy through the living things of an ecosystem. It begins with producers, which turn sunlight into chemical energy stored as glucose, a sugar, through {{ref:nature-eco-190}}. Respiration reverses the process, releasing the energy for use. Organisms are organized into producers and consumers in food chains, and those chains stack into trophic pyramids. What happens higher up depends on the base. Secondary production by herbivores and by organisms that break down dead matter depends on primary productivity. Producers fix carbon at similar rates across ecosystems. Ecosystems differ instead in how that energy moves to higher levels. Overall, energy flow depends on primary productivity together with temperature, water and light.

nature-eco-363.title: The marine food web: life's chain in the sea
nature-eco-363.text: Coastal waters cover about 8 per cent of the ocean but account for about half of all ocean productivity. They are a rich corner of the marine food web, the food web of life in the sea. Its base is phytoplankton, single-celled algae and plant-like organisms. Zooplankton, tiny drifting animals that eat them, form the second trophic level. A typical ocean food chain runs from phytoplankton to herbivorous zooplankton, carnivorous zooplankton, a filter feeder and then a predatory vertebrate. Forage fish sit in the middle of ocean food webs as the main prey of larger fish, seabirds and mammals. Microorganisms play much bigger roles in the marine web than was once thought. The web is vulnerable from below. {{ref:nature-eco-248}} damages pteropods, small sea snails, and brittle stars at the base of Arctic food webs, threatening those webs from the bottom up.

nature-eco-346.title: Ecological pyramids: picturing life's levels
nature-eco-346.text: In a pond at any moment, the phytoplankton weigh less than the fish and insects above them. They reproduce fast but live briefly. An ecological pyramid is a diagram showing the biomass or productivity at each trophic level of an ecosystem, with producers at the base. It comes in three forms. A pyramid of energy shows the energy kept as new biomass at each level. A pyramid of biomass shows the living matter present. A pyramid of numbers counts individuals. Energy pyramids are normally upright. Their base is narrow to begin with: only 1 to 2 percent of the Sun's energy is absorbed by {{ref:nature-eco-190}} and turned into food. Biomass pyramids can be inverted in the sea, as the pond shows. Number pyramids can invert too, when many beetles feed on one tree. Charles Elton developed the pyramid of numbers in 1927. Bodenheimer expressed it in biomass in 1938, and the energy pyramid draws on Hutchinson and Lindeman (1942).

nature-eco-300.title: Trophic dynamics: following energy through feeding
nature-eco-300.text: In 1942 Raymond Lindeman published a landmark paper on trophic dynamics, the study of how energy passes from one part of an ecosystem to another through feeding. That paper introduced the trophic level concept. Assigning each organism to one level is imprecise, though. Omnivores, which eat both plants and animals, feed at several levels. Research finds that distinct levels do exist. Above the herbivores, however, food webs are better described as a tangle of omnivores.

nature-eco-343.title: Ecological efficiency: why energy thins at each step
nature-eco-343.text: Every calorie of energy spent growing soy returns 415% in edible calories. For shrimp, the return is 0.9%. Ecological efficiency explains much of that gap. It measures how efficiently energy passes from one trophic level to the next, and the answer is: poorly. Each level's net production is usually only about 10% of the level below. Energy leaks away at three steps: death not caused by predators, egestion (food passed out undigested) and respiration. Halving at each of the three steps leaves about one-eighth, roughly ten percent. Formally, it combines exploitation, assimilation and net production efficiencies, and it equals consumer production divided by prey production. The lesson for diets is direct. It is more energy-efficient to eat from lower trophic levels. Potatoes return 123% and corn 250%, while chicken returns 18.1% and grass-fed beef 6.7%. Food takes real energy to make. In 1999, 10.5% of the 28,400 terawatt-hours of energy used in the US went into food production.

nature-eco-381.title: Ambush or chase: how predators hunt
nature-eco-381.text: Some predators wait; others chase. Sit-and-wait hunting suits dense, mobile prey and predators with low energy needs. Wide foraging costs more energy and suits prey that is sparse or stays put. In social predation, groups such as wolves or hyenas cooperate to kill animals as large as buffalo. Predators also differ in how wide their menu is. Specialists such as the Eurasian lynx hunt few prey types, while generalists such as leopards take at least 100 species.

nature-eco-382.title: Predator–prey coevolution: an evolutionary arms race
nature-eco-382.text: Bats evolved echolocation, finding insects by the echoes of their calls, and some insects evolved the ability to hear those calls. That is predator–prey coevolution: an arms race in which predators and prey evolve adaptations that counter each other. Prey defenses include camouflage, mimicry (resembling something else) and warning others of predators.

nature-eco-306.title: Fractional trophic levels: feeding between the steps
nature-eco-306.text: A trophic level need not be a whole number. Many organisms feed at more than one level, so a consumer's level is one plus the diet-weighted average level of what it eats. Most fish and other marine consumers fall between 2.0 and 5.0. A value of 5.0 occurs in apex predators such as polar bears and orcas. The level can even be read from body tissue. Stable nitrogen isotopes, forms of nitrogen with slightly different weights, rise about 3–4‰ (parts per thousand) at each level.

nature-eco-307.title: Fishing down the food web: tracking the catch's trophic level
nature-eco-307.text: In the northwest and west-central Atlantic, the average trophic level of the catch peaked at 3.4 in 1970 and fell to 2.9 by 1994, Pauly and colleagues report. Catches had shifted from cod and haddock to shrimp and herring. This measure, the mean trophic level of fisheries catch, averages over all the fish caught in an area in a year. It tracks fishing pressure. Early reports found steep declines in it, a process called {{ref:nature-res-054}}. In 2000 Pauly and others built an index to check whether falling levels are matched by rising catches. Later work found that mean trophic levels in catches and surveys have not declined globally. That suggests the decline is not worldwide.

nature-eco-308.title: Tritrophic interactions: plant, herbivore and predator together
nature-eco-308.text: Studying plants and herbivores alone can mislead. Plants and predators together can shape how fast herbivore populations grow. A tritrophic interaction links three trophic levels at once, such as plant, herbivore and predator. Even a plant's shape matters. It can change how well the plant resists herbivores by affecting the herbivores' enemies.

nature-eco-299.title: Are complex food webs more stable?
nature-eco-299.text: Are food webs with more species and more links more stable? Ecologists have not settled the question. Two measures frame it. Connectance is the fraction of all possible feeding links that actually occur in a network. Complexity is sometimes defined as the number of species multiplied by connectance, though that definition has been criticized. Mathematical models challenged the idea that complexity brings stability. Later studies found that it holds in real systems after all.

nature-eco-360.title: Grazers and browsers: two ways to eat plants
nature-eco-360.text: Cows graze and moose browse. Grazers eat mostly grass, while browsers eat tree leaves and twigs, and these are the two main herbivore feeding strategies. A land mammal counts as a grazer if at least 90% of its forage is grass, and a browser if at least 90% is tree leaves and twigs. Anything in between is mixed-feeding. Size matters too. Small herbivores pick high-quality forage, while larger ones are less selective. Kleiber's law says larger animals need less food per unit of body weight than smaller ones.

nature-eco-361.title: Plant defenses: tolerating and resisting herbivores
nature-eco-361.text: Many plant-eaters eat a mix of plants, balancing their nutrients and avoiding too much of any one defensive chemical. Those chemicals are one kind of plant defense against herbivory: any trait that improves a plant's survival or reproduction when animals feed on it. Defenses fall into two kinds. Tolerance means withstanding damage without losing fitness. Resistance means reducing how much damage is done. Herbivores push back. They choose which plants to eat, adapt their own bodies, or modify the plant.

nature-eco-354.title: Food chain length: why chains stay short
nature-eco-354.text: A salad yields more energy per pound than an animal that ate lettuce. The reason lies in food chain length, the number of feeding links between a consumer and the base of its food chain. Generally only about ten percent of the energy at one trophic level passes to the next. The rest is used up in metabolism, the chemistry of staying alive. Food chains usually have no more than five trophic levels. Ecologists offer several explanations for where chains stop. Length may grow with ecosystem volume, be capped by energy loss at each level, or reflect habitat type.

nature-eco-288.title: Top-down and bottom-up: what controls an ecosystem
nature-eco-288.text: Without top carnivores, herbivores could multiply and eat all the plants. If plant populations crash instead, herbivores decline, and then carnivores decline too. Those two chains of cause are top-down and bottom-up control, the two ways an ecosystem's structure is shaped. One works from above, through predators. The other works from below, through how much energy plants bring in. Energy captured by plants passes to herbivores, then carnivores, then top carnivores, and the total shrinks at each higher level. Trophic dynamics, the transfer of energy and nutrients between organisms, links the two. Predators can dramatically shift which species dominate on land and at sea. The balance between the two controls is a major research question. An ecosystem need not be one or the other. A marine system may be bottom-up, then come under top-down control during fishing. Herbivores also reach down into the soil. Herbivory can speed the breakdown of fallen leaves and the cycling of nutrients by changing litter quality and vegetation.

nature-eco-338.title: Apparent competition: rivals through a shared predator
nature-eco-338.text: Introduced snowshoe hares in Newfoundland may have shrunk the range of native arctic hares, not by eating their food but by boosting their shared predator, the lynx. This is apparent competition: an indirect contest in which two unrelated prey species affect each other through a shared predator. If one prey species booms, its predator increases and then hunts both prey more heavily, so the other species declines. Robert D. Holt coined the term in 1977. Conservation scientists see human introductions of predators, or of food subsidies such as garbage, as an extreme, one-sided form of it.

nature-eco-367.title: Plant-pollinator networks: shared structure, shared fate
nature-eco-367.text: The webs linking plants to their pollinators have a strikingly similar structure on different continents, even with entirely different species. A plant-pollinator network is this web of mutualistic links. Models suggest its structure reduces competition between pollinators and strengthens ecosystem stability. That strength has a dark side. Pollinators survive harsh conditions together, but they collapse simultaneously once conditions pass a critical point. The network's structure may shape how pollinator communities respond as conditions grow harsher.
